terms.definition: The 1000 Genomes Project produced a public catalog of human genetic variation from diverse populations, including phased haplotypes and population allele frequencies, widely used as an imputation reference, allele-frequency panel, and ancestry benchmark before larger resources...

Absolute risk is the probability that an individual who is disease-free at baseline will develop the outcome over a defined follow-up period, often expressed as a percentage. It contrasts with relative measures that compare groups.
Addition of acetyl groups—classically on histone lysines altering chromatin compaction.
Chromosome with centromere near one end and a prominent short arm (human acrocentrics carry rDNA repeats).

Designed for a specific immediate purpose rather than from a pre-specified, general analysis plan. In GWAS reporting, ad hoc steps are often practical but should be clearly distinguished from pre-registered primary analyses.
Trait or allele frequency change raising fitness in an environment—interpreted cautiously from GWAS hits.

Adaptive burden tests choose which rare variants to include or how to weight them using the data—rather than fixing a single minor allele frequency or functional mask a priori—then test association on the resulting collapsed score. They belong to the “adaptive burden” class in...

The additive model codes genotype as the count of a reference allele (0, 1, 2) and assumes the phenotype mean shifts linearly with that count—each additional allele changes risk or trait mean by the same amount on the modeled scale.
Purine nucleobase pairing with thymine in DNA (uracil in RNA).
Central energy currency and nucleotide substrate kinases couple to phosphorylation signaling.

Admixture refers to the mixing of ancestry from previously separated populations, producing genomes with segments derived from multiple ancestral sources. In GWAS datasets, admixture is reflected in continuous rather than discrete ancestry patterns.

Admixture mapping tests association between a trait and local genetic ancestry—the estimated proportion of each chromosome inherited from each ancestral source population—rather than testing individual SNPs alone. It can detect loci where ancestry segments from a specific sour...
US census and health-research label for Americans with African ancestry; genetically heterogeneous.
Coarse label for probabilistic genetic ties to a broad world region in biobanks and reference panels; distinct from social identity alone.

An AI agent is a system that uses a language or multimodal model together with a control loop: it plans steps, calls tools (code, APIs, retrieval), observes results, and iterates until a goal is met—rather than producing a single static completion from one prompt.
Model selection score trading fit (log likelihood) against parameter count; useful for comparing nested and some non-nested regression and mixed models.

All of Us is a U.S. precision medicine cohort that recruits participants reflecting national diversity in ancestry, geography, and health status, collecting genomic data (genotyping and whole-genome sequencing), electronic health records, surveys, and physical measurements for...
An allele is one of the alternative forms of a genetic variant at a genomic position; for a bi-allelic site, an individual's diploid genotype is the pair of alleles they carry (e.g. AA, AG, GG).
Proportion or count of a given allele among chromosomes in a defined sample.
Allele sharing describes the extent to which two individuals carry the same alleles at one locus or across many loci. It may be summarized using IBS-based or IBD-based measures depending on context.
Different causal variants at the same locus can produce the same or overlapping phenotypes.
Common secondary structure motif in proteins formed by hydrogen-bonded backbone coils.
The alternative allele (ALT) is any non-reference allele at a site relative to the chosen reference genome. Multi-allelic sites list one REF and multiple ALT alleles.
Assertion departing from null—non-zero dosage effect for at least one allele encoding.

Alternative polyadenylation is the use of multiple cleavage and polyadenylation sites in a pre-mRNA, producing isoforms with different 3′ untranslated regions or, less often, different coding sequences. It alters mRNA stability, localization, and translation regulation.

Alternative splicing is the production of multiple mature RNA isoforms from one gene through different exon inclusion, intron retention, or splice-site usage. It expands the transcriptome beyond a single protein-coding form per locus and varies by tissue and condition.

Ambient RNA is extracellular or lysate RNA that is captured in a single-cell droplet or well together with a cell’s own transcriptome, contaminating profiles and inflating apparent expression of highly abundant transcripts outside their true cell of origin.
Coarse label for probabilistic genetic ties to a broad world region in biobanks and reference panels; distinct from social identity alone.
Partitioning total variance into between-group and within-group components via F-tests; common in lab and pathway-style factor experiments adjacent to genetics.
Mitosis/meiosis stage where sister chromatids or homologs separate toward poles.

The ATC classification assigns hierarchical codes to medicines by organ system (anatomical main group), therapeutic and pharmacological subgroup, and chemical substance. It is maintained by the WHO Collaborating Centre for Drug Statistics Methodology and is widely used in pres...
Allele inferred to match the most recent common ancestor of a site—may differ from reference assembly allele.

Genetic ancestry describes the proportion of an individual’s genome inherited from specified source populations (e.g. European, African, East Asian) or along continuous axes of variation. It is inferred from genotypes via PCA, supervised assignment, or local ancestry along the...
Variant with strong frequency contrast across populations used to infer ancestry proportions.
Cell or organism with abnormal chromosome count not a whole multiple of the haploid set.
Gain or loss of individual chromosomes (e.g. trisomy) versus euploid sets.
Calendar epoch for years after the conventional anchor; dating metadata in archaeology-genetics papers.
Process of attaching structured labels to sequences or variants—coordinates, genes, consequences, regulatory tracks, and scores—so downstream tools can interpret raw genomics data.

ANNOVAR is a software toolkit for annotating genetic variants against gene models, population frequency resources, predicted functional effects, and other external databases. It accepts variant positions and alleles, then adds consequence labels and database-derived context fo...

Antagonistic pleiotropy occurs when a genetic variant increases fitness or benefit for one trait while harming another (e.g. early-life advantage vs. late-life disease), a classic idea in the evolution of aging and trade-offs.
Study of humans across biology, culture, and prehistory; contextualizes genetic sampling frames.
Earlier onset or increased severity in successive generations, classically discussed for some repeat-expansion disorders (interpreted cautiously).
An anticodon is a triplet of nucleotides in a transfer RNA (tRNA) molecule that base-pairs with a complementary mRNA codon during translation, helping deliver the correct amino acid to the ribosome.

The antisense strand of DNA is the template strand read by RNA polymerase to produce RNA complementary to the non-template “sense” strand. In common lab usage, an antisense oligonucleotide or transcript is complementary to a target RNA and can modulate its expression or splicing.
Template DNA strand read 3′→5′ to synthesize RNA opposite in polarity to the resulting transcript.
Programmed cell death executed by intracellular pathways; relevant to tissue homeostasis and some disease mechanisms.
Likelihood-free inference accepting simulations matching summary statistics—occasionally used in demo/history inference adjacent to genetics.

Apptainer is the open-source container runtime that succeeded Singularity under the Linux Foundation umbrella; it emphasizes secure, unprivileged execution on multi-user HPC systems and remains compatible with the same image workflows many genomics groups adopted under the ear...

The area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC) summarizes how well a predictor—such as a polygenic risk score—separates cases from controls across all possible classification thresholds. AUC 0.5 is chance discrimination; 1.0 is perfect.
Average of observed values—phenotype mean imputation and covariate centering reference point.
How individuals or families enter a study (e.g. via affected probands) can bias apparent inheritance patterns and allele frequencies.
Broad US OMB racial grouping spanning diverse West, Central, South, and East Asian ancestries.
ATAC-seq inserts sequencing adapters into open chromatin regions using a transposase, producing a genome-wide map of chromatin accessibility with relatively low input requirements.
Non-random pairing by phenotype or genotype—biases relatedness structure and heritability estimates.

An attention mechanism reweights inputs (tokens, positions, or features) based on learned compatibility scores, producing context-dependent representations; self-attention relates all positions to each other and is the core of transformer architectures.

An autoencoder is a neural network trained to map inputs through a low-dimensional bottleneck (encoder) and reconstruct them (decoder), minimizing reconstruction error; it learns a compressed representation useful for denoising, anomaly detection, or pretraining.
An autosome is any chromosome that is not a sex chromosome. Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes; the remaining pair comprises the X and (when present) Y sex chromosomes.
Homozygosity for haplotypes inherited identically by descent within an individual—elevated in consanguinity or isolates.
Amplicon or capture sequencing of immunoglobulin rearrangements reconstructing clonotypes and somatic hypermutation—immune repertoire layer orthogonal to germline GWAS.
Mating offspring to one parental lineage to recover a specific background while retaining a locus of interest.

Backpropagation is the algorithm that computes gradients of a loss with respect to all neural network weights by applying the chain rule backward through the computation graph, enabling efficient gradient descent training of deep models.
Low-copy plasmid clone (~100–300 kb) used for physical mapping and sequencing.
Virus infecting bacteria; historical workhorse in molecular genetics cloning (phage vectors).
Condensed inactive X chromatin visible in female somatic nuclei reflecting X inactivation.
Translating raw instrument signals (fluorescence or ionic current) into nucleotide calls with per-base quality scores feeding aligners and genotypers.

A base pair (bp) is one rung of the DNA double helix: a hydrogen-bonded pair of nucleotides (A–T or G–C) on opposite strands. Genomic distances, variant positions, and interval lengths are usually counted in bp, kilobases (kb), or megabases (Mb).

In neural-network training, a batch (often a minibatch) is the subset of examples whose losses are averaged to form one gradient estimate for an optimizer step; batch size trades off noise in updates against memory use and wall-clock time.

A batch effect is systematic technical variation associated with processing groups such as plates, centers, reagent lots, or genotyping waves rather than biology. It can alter call rates, allele frequencies, or phenotype measurements.
Bayesian evidence ratio comparing marginal likelihoods of two models or hypotheses; appears in fine-mapping and variant prioritization priors.
Identity relating posterior odds to prior odds times the likelihood ratio—conceptual backbone of Bayesian fine-mapping and colocalization priors.
Marginal probability of data under a model ∫ p(data|θ)p(θ)dθ; larger values favor models in Bayes factors.
Full posterior inference for parameters or models via priors, likelihoods, and simulation; complements frequency-based GWAS.
Penalized log-likelihood with stronger complexity penalty than AIC; used for model comparison in moderated settings.
Bayesian non-parametric estimate of effective population size over time from gene genealogies.
Framework treating parameters with probability distributions updated by data; guides some pathogenicity and fine-mapping posteriors.

BED/BIM/FAM is the classic PLINK 1 binary genotype trio: .bed stores sample-by-variant genotypes in compact binary form, .bim stores variant metadata, and .fam stores sample metadata. In GWAS practice it usually represents hard-called genotypes rather than posterior dosages, a...

BEDPE (BED paired-end) extends BED to represent pairs of genomic intervals in one record, such as structural-variant breakpoints or paired interaction anchors. It is commonly used when one interval is insufficient to describe an event.
Years counting backward from the conventional anchor before year 1 CE.
Years before CE 1950 per radiocarbon convention; standard ancient DNA age reporting.
Secular label equivalent to BC in scholarly writing.
Single-trial {0,1} model with success probability p—building block for binomial counts of reference alleles.
Continuous (0,1) family common as allele-frequency priors and rate parameters.
Extended sheet secondary structure stabilized by backbone hydrogen bonds between segments.
Compound count model mixing binomial with beta rate—overdispersed alternative to plain binomial read counts.

BGEN is a binary file format (Oxford / UK Biobank style) for storing large-scale genotype or imputed-dosage data compactly, including probabilities or dosages per sample and variant. PLINK 2 documents import from and export to BGEN alongside other formats.

A biallelic variant is a site represented with exactly two alleles in the analysis—typically a reference allele and one alternative allele—so each diploid genotype is a pair drawn from those two states. Many GWAS arrays, imputed panels, and summary-statistic pipelines assume b...

Bias is a systematic deviation of an estimator's expected value from the true parameter. In GWAS, major classes include confounding (e.g. population structure, cryptic relatedness), measurement error, selection and participation effects, and analysis-induced biases such as mod...
Distribution or histogram with two dominant modes—can signal mixture populations or dichotomized liability.

BAM is the compressed binary representation of SAM records for aligned sequencing reads, designed for efficient storage, indexing, and random access. It is typically accompanied by a .bai index for region-based queries.
Sum of n independent Bernoulli trials—idealized model for unrelated diploid binomial draws under HWE.
Biobank Japan is a large hospital-based biobank with genotype and phenotype data from Japanese participants, designed to support disease genetics and precision medicine research.
Bioinformatics develops algorithms, software, and databases to store, align, annotate, and interpret large-scale biological sequence and omics data.

Biological Causality refers to claims about the actual molecular, cellular, or physiological mechanism linking genetic variation (or an intervention) to phenotype—which gene or regulatory element is altered, in which context, and through which mediators—as opposed to statistic...
Interbreeding group modeled as sharing a gene pool.
Covalent attachment of biotin to proteins as a regulatory or tagging modification.
Bisulfite sequencing treats DNA with bisulfite to convert unmethylated cytosines, then sequences the result to map cytosine methylation (often CpG) at base resolution.

Bonferroni correction controls the family-wise error rate by testing each of m hypotheses at level α/m (or equivalently comparing p-values to α/m). It is simple and assumption-light but conservative when tests are correlated—typical in dense LD—so GWAS more often uses permutat...

A Brisbane plot is a genome-wide scatter visualization where each point is an approximately independent association signal (for example after linkage disequilibrium-aware clumping or conditional analysis), plotted against chromosomal position. The vertical axis encodes local d...
Broad-sense heritability is the proportion of phenotypic variance attributable to all genetic sources of variation, including additive, dominance, and interaction effects. It is commonly denoted H^2.
Archaeological period of bronze metallurgy common in European and Asian aDNA time series.

BED is a tab-delimited interval format from UCSC for representing genomic regions such as peaks, genes, or custom annotation tracks. The first three columns are chromosome, start, and end coordinates, with optional additional columns for names, scores, strand, and other fields.

A burden test collapses rare variant genotypes in a region into a single genetic score per individual—often the count or weighted sum of minor alleles meeting annotation or frequency filters—and tests association with the phenotype. It assumes effects are directionally similar...

C is a low-level procedural language that underpins much systems software and many long-standing bioinformatics libraries. PLINK, SAMtools/htslib-family code, and numerical libraries often expose C APIs or are wrapped from Python or R for GWAS pipelines.

C++ extends C with classes, templates, and standard-library facilities. Performance-critical genomics tools—statistical genetics engines, imputation backends, and sequence I/O—are often implemented in C++ for speed and then called from higher-level languages or distributed as...

Calibration describes how well predicted risk or probability matches observed outcome frequencies in the target population—often assessed with calibration plots, the Hosmer–Lemeshow test, calibration slope and intercept, or Brier-related decomposition. A model can be well disc...
Call rate is the proportion of genotypes successfully assigned by the genotyping platform or analysis pipeline. It can be calculated per sample or per variant.
Paleozoic period of early animal diversification—deep backdrop for metazoan gene evolution.
Robustness of phenotype to genetic or environmental perturbation—evolutionary genetics context for GxE.

A candidate cis-regulatory element (cCRE) is a genomic interval in the ENCODE Registry of candidate cis-Regulatory Elements: a catalog that integrates DNase-seq, histone modifications, CTCF binding, and related assays to nominate regulatory DNA with standardized labels (e.g. p...

A canonical transcript is the representative splice isoform a database or tool uses as the default for a gene—often for displaying consequences, longest coding sequence, or community-curated “principal” isoforms. The exact rule varies by resource (e.g. Ensembl, RefSeq, MANE),...

CAGE (cap analysis of gene expression) maps the 5′ ends of capped RNAs genome-wide, usually by short-tag sequencing, to infer transcription start sites (TSSs) and promoter usage. Large atlases (e.g. FANTOM) use CAGE to refine where transcription initiates relative to annotated...
Radiocarbon dating with calibration curves converting C-14 activity to calendar ranges.

CARMA is a Bayesian fine-mapping model designed for GWAS meta-analysis summary data, explicitly handling the structure of combined studies when inferring causal configurations and variant-level posteriors at a locus.

Case-control imbalance means a binary-trait study has far fewer cases than controls, often by orders of magnitude in biobank-scale analyses of rare diseases. In that regime, standard asymptotic logistic-regression tests can become miscalibrated, especially for low-frequency va...

A case-control design compares unrelated affected cases to unaffected controls, estimating genotype frequencies or odds ratios. It is the dominant GWAS design for binary disease traits; controls should reflect the same underlying population as cases to limit stratification.
Discrete outcome with arbitrary K unordered categories—multinomial slice at n=1.

A causal configuration is a specific assignment of which variants in a locus are treated as causal (versus non-causal) within a fine-mapping model. Bayesian methods such as FINEMAP place a prior over the space of configurations and update it with association data to obtain pos...
Purposefully joining design, assumptions, and estimands to support cause–effect claims—Mendelian randomization operationalizes genetics pieces.

terms.term: Causal Machine Learning for Single-Cell Genomics
terms.definition: Causal machine learning for single-cell genomics aims to estimate perturbation effects, counterfactual cell states, or regulatory structure from high-dimensional single-cell data while addressing confounding, batch structure, and missing interventions. Approaches include optim...

Causality is the relation by which changes in one process or variable bring about, or help explain, changes in another—distinct from mere association. In genetics, claims are often split into statistical causal identification (what designs and assumptions justify a causal esti...
Immortalized or long-lived cultured cells representing a lineage; used for functional assays of GWAS variants.

Cell villages are co-cultures in which induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines from many donors are differentiated together in the same dish, as opposed to parallel uni-cultures per donor. The design enables population-scale cellular phenotyping with shared environmental co...

Cell-type annotation is the process of assigning biologically meaningful labels to clusters or neighborhoods in single-cell data—manually from marker genes, or computationally by reference mapping, label transfer, or classifiers—so that analyses (including sc-eQTL) are interpr...
Era including primate radiation and the Quaternary glacial cycles shaping human demography.

In survival and time-to-event analyses, censoring means the event time is not fully observed for an individual: follow-up stops before the event, the event is not yet recorded in the database, or (in some designs) only interval information is available. Standard estimators lik...

The centimorgan (cM) is a unit of genetic (recombination) distance: two loci separated by 1 cM have roughly a 1% chance of being separated by crossing over in one meiosis. Physical distance per cM varies across the genome and populations.

The central dogma of molecular biology describes the usual flow of information from DNA to RNA to protein: DNA is transcribed to RNA, and RNA is translated into a polypeptide. Reverse transcription and prion-like templating are known exceptions in some contexts.
A Central Processing Unit (CPU) is the general-purpose processor that executes operating-system tasks and most application code, typically with fewer but more flexible cores than a GPU.

The centromere is the chromosomal region where sister chromatids attach to the spindle during cell division; it often lies within repetitive DNA and divides each chromosome into short (p) and long (q) arms in cytogenetic notation.

A chain file stores pairwise whole-genome alignment blocks between assemblies and is used to map coordinates from one reference build to another. It encodes aligned segments, gap structure, and chromosome-level context for lift-over operations.

Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting asks a language model to emit intermediate reasoning steps before a final answer—often improving multi-step problems in math, logic, or structured extraction—at the cost of longer generations and sensitivity to prompt phrasing.
Transitional copper-and-stone period before full Bronze Age in regional sequences.
Sum of squared standard normals—reference for Pearson tests and many LRTs when df fixed.
Individual with cells of more than one distinct genotype (tetragametic, bone marrow transplant, fetal microchimerism).

Chromatin is the complex of genomic DNA with histones and other proteins that packages the genome inside the nucleus. Its compaction and chemical modifications influence accessibility for transcription and repair.

A chromatin accessibility quantitative trait locus (caQTL) is a genetic variant associated with open chromatin signal—typically peak counts or accessibility scores from ATAC-seq, DNase-seq, or similar assays—in a given cell type or tissue.
ChIP-seq maps genome-wide binding of proteins such as transcription factors and histone modifications by immunoprecipitating chromatin fragments and sequencing the associated DNA.

A chromosome is a single long DNA molecule packaged with proteins; humans have 22 pairs of autosomes and two sex chromosomes per diploid cell. Cytogenetic labels (e.g. 1–22, X, Y) and sequence coordinates refer to distinct chromosome copies in analysis pipelines.
Ligation-based assay quantifying contact frequency between two chosen loci in fixed nuclei—foundational for 3C family methods.
Multiplexed extension of 3C targeting many primer pairs simultaneously to map a focused interaction network among selected fragments.

In this on-chip 4C design, a single bait viewpoint is hybridized against targets on a microarray so contacts genome-wide are read out via microarray capture—different from circularized 4C-seq (Circularized chromosome conformation capture (4C-seq)), which uses sequencing of cir...
Subdivision of a stage; finer than epoch in formal stratigraphic tables.
Chromosome with no free ends (typical bacterial); contrasts with linear eukaryotic chromosomes protected by telomeres.
4C-seq uses circularized ligation products to enrich one-versus-all contact profiles from a single viewpoint (bait), distinct from the older microarray “4C-on-chip” design.
Regulatory effect on linked sequences on the same DNA molecule (promoters, enhancers).

A cis-regulatory element (CRE) is a noncoding DNA segment on the same chromosome as its target gene(s) that modulates transcription—classically promoters, enhancers, silencers, and insulators—through binding of transcription factors and chromatin regulators. “Cis” contrasts wi...
Rank between phylum and order grouping orders with shared ancestry.

Classification accuracy is the fraction of predictions that match the observed class labels among all predictions (correct classifications divided by total). For binary outcomes with unequal prevalence or unequal misclassification costs, accuracy can be misleading even when di...
Cells or organisms derived asexually from a common ancestor (molecularly near-identical) or, in older usage, a recombinant DNA clone carried in a vector.

terms.term: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats
terms.definition: CRISPR–Cas systems are programmable nucleases (and related editors) used to cut or modify DNA or RNA at targeted sequences, enabling high-throughput perturbation screens and precise genome engineering in cells and model organisms.

Coalescent theory models the backward-in-time merging of gene copies into common ancestors, yielding a stochastic genealogy whose structure depends on effective population size, migration, selection, and recombination. It underlies many simulators and estimators of demography...

A skill is a packaged bundle of instructions, conventions, or resources (often markdown and small scripts) that an AI coding assistant loads to specialize its behavior for a task or repo—without changing the base model weights. Skills extend default behavior the way project do...
Gene with a protein product (may include UTRs and introns).
Both alleles at a locus are fully reflected in the heterozygous phenotype (neither is recessive to the other).
In association testing, a parameterization where heterozygotes have their own mean distinct from either homozygote class.
A codon is a contiguous triplet of nucleotides in mRNA (or the corresponding DNA coding sequence) that specifies one amino acid or a translation stop signal during protein synthesis.
Generic multiplier of a predictor in a model—allele dosage effect in GWAS is a coefficient on an additive coding scale.

The coefficient of determination, denoted R², is the proportion of variance in the outcome explained by a regression fit on a given sample—typically 1 minus the ratio of residual to total sum of squares for ordinary least squares. For nonlinear or regularized models, R² may us...

Probability an allele chosen at random in one individual is identical by descent (IBD) to an allele drawn at the same locus from another individual; under standard diploid pedigree conventions it equals twice the Kinship Coefficient.

The coefficient of relationship is the probability that an allele chosen at random from one individual is identical by descent (IBD) to an allele at the same locus in another—the same quantity many papers denote r. In this dictionary the main discussion is under Coefficient of...

A cohort is a defined group of individuals assembled for study, often with shared recruitment, phenotyping, and genotyping protocols. Prospective cohorts follow participants over time; cross-sectional biobanks are large disease-agnostic cohorts used for many GWAS.
A cohort study follows a defined Cohort over time, recording exposures and outcomes; prospective and retrospective variants underpin many biomarker and PRS prognosis papers.

Collider bias arises when two variables both influence whether an individual is included in an analysis (or stratum), and conditioning on that inclusion opens a non-causal path between them, inducing spurious association or attenuating true effects.

Colocalization tests whether two association signals (e.g. a GWAS trait and an eQTL in the same region) plausibly share the same causal variant, often by comparing posterior probabilities over causal configurations in a locus (e.g. coloc, eCAVIAR).
Integrative pathogenicity score combining many functional annotations to rank SNVs and small indels; higher scores suggest more deleterious impact.

A common ancestor is an individual, population, or taxon from which two or more descendants inherit shared genetic material; in coalescent and phylogenetic models, lineages trace backward in time until they meet at ancestral nodes representing those shared origins.
Secular label equivalent to AD for calendar years in publications.

A common variant is a genetic variant with relatively high population frequency, often defined using a minor allele frequency threshold such as greater than 1% or 5%. Many classical GWAS are optimized to detect associations with common variants.
DNA synthesized from RNA (reverse transcription); synthesized mature transcript lacks introns.

A complex disease (or complex trait) is influenced by many genetic variants of small to moderate effect together with environment and behavior, rather than following simple Mendelian inheritance from one or a few genes.
A trait influenced by many genetic and environmental factors; typically polygenic with no single Mendelian locus explaining most risk.

A compound heterozygote carries two different pathogenic (or tested) alleles at the same gene—typically on opposite haplotypes (in trans)—so each chromosome copy bears a distinct variant. Resolving compound heterozygosity usually requires family data or phasing because unphase...
A compute cluster is a group of networked machines (nodes) that work together to run jobs in parallel, typically managed by a scheduler such as Slurm.
Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) is NVIDIA's parallel computing platform and programming model for running general-purpose code on GPUs.

Conda is a cross-language package and environment manager popular in scientific computing; conda environments collect pinned binaries (Python, R, C++ libs) from channels or conda-forge, complementing pip-only stacks when compiled omics dependencies are required.

Conditional association analysis tests whether a variant remains associated with a trait after accounting for genotype at one or more other variants—usually the lead SNP(s) in the same locus—so secondary signals can be distinguished from a single shared haplotype effect.
Probability of an event given another—enters haplotype phase models and lineage likelihoods.
Frequentist interval from a recipe covering the true parameter under repeated sampling at a stated confidence level—not equal to Bayesian credible intervals.
SEM submodel testing hypothesized factor loadings—used in psychometric GWAS endophenotypes.
Family closed under posteriors with a specific likelihood—simplifies closed-form updating in some Bayesian models.
Prior chosen so posterior stays in the same parametric family for a given likelihood—pedagogic and some hierarchical genetic count models.
Union between related individuals elevating autozygosity and recessive risk.
Close biological relatedness between mates measured socially or via pedigree.

Contamination is the presence of DNA from more than one source in a sample, causing distorted genotype calls and abnormal allele balance or heterozygosity patterns. It may arise during collection, extraction, library preparation, or array processing.

In large language model systems, context is the information the model can attend to in a single inference—typically the concatenation (or structured packing) of system instructions, user input, retrieved passages, tool outputs, and (in chat setups) prior turns. It is the worki...

Context engineering is the practice of selecting, structuring, and maintaining the information placed in a model’s working context—retrieved passages, tool outputs, memories, structured state, and conversation history—so that the model has the right facts in the right order an...

The context window is the maximum number of tokens a language model can attend to in a single forward pass—covering system instructions, user input, retrieved documents, and (for chat models) prior turns—beyond which text must be truncated, summarized, or split across calls.
A contig is a continuous assembled stretch of sequence without gaps, built from overlapping reads or clones. Reference genomes are organized into contigs and scaffolds that map to chromosomes.
Law given by density over uncountable support—describes many polygenic liability constructions.
Flat density over a bounded interval—simple prior and permutation reference baseline.
Controls-only HWE refers to testing Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium in controls rather than in the full sample or in cases. This practice helps separate technical artifacts from true disease association.

A convolutional neural network (CNN) applies learned local filters across spatial or sequential inputs (images, 1D sequence windows, or multi-channel tensors), pooling or striding to build hierarchical features; weight sharing makes CNNs data-efficient for grid-like or local-m...
Orthologs produced by an allopolyploidization or lineage-specific duplication followed by speciation—plant and ancient polyploid context.
Early copper metallurgy phase in some cultural chronologies.

A copy number variant is a structural variant that changes the number of copies of a genomic segment, usually through deletion or duplication. CNVs can range from small events affecting a gene to very large chromosomal segments.
Standardized linear association measure between paired variables; baseline QC and some phenotype correlation structure checks.

Coverage is the amount of sequencing data overlapping a genomic position or region, often summarized as mean depth across the genome, exome, or targeted panel. It is commonly described in x units such as 30x coverage.

A semiparametric regression model for time-to-event data that relates covariates to the hazard multiplicatively while leaving the baseline hazard unspecified. Proportional hazards means the hazard ratio between individuals differing only by a covariate is constant over time; u...
GC-rich region with elevated CpG dinucleotide density; often unmethylated around promoters in somatic cells.
A CPU core is an individual execution unit inside a CPU that can run instructions independently, allowing one processor package to handle multiple tasks in parallel.

CRAM is a reference-based compressed alignment format that stores sequencing read alignments more compactly than BAM by encoding differences relative to a reference sequence. It is standardized in the HTS specifications and supports indexing for random access.

A credible set (often a 95% credible set) is the smallest set of variants whose posterior inclusion probabilities sum to a target coverage under a Bayesian fine-mapping model. It summarizes uncertainty about which SNPs might be causal at a locus, unlike a single “lead” SNP or...
Spanning multiple ancestries or geographic origins—common in multi-biobank GWAS language.

Cross-ancestry genetic correlation quantifies how similar the genetic architecture of a trait is between populations—often estimated from GWAS summary statistics as a correlation of causal or tagging effects across SNPs (trans-ethnic ρ-type estimators). High correlation sugges...

Cross-population effect heterogeneity describes differences in the estimated (or true) causal effect of a variant or locus on a trait between ancestry groups—distinct from discovering different loci altogether (genetic heterogeneity) or from statistical artifacts of LD and tag...
Data splitting scheme training models on subsets and evaluating on held-out folds; standard for PRS tuning and prediction benchmarks.
One partition of data used alternately as validation while other folds train—k-fold CV optimizes hyperparameters without an external set.
Crossing over is the exchange of DNA between homologous chromosomes during meiosis, creating recombinant chromosomes. Its rate and placement shape linkage disequilibrium across generations.

Cryptic relatedness is unrecognized familial relationship among study participants that is not captured in the recorded pedigree or study metadata. It is usually inferred from genome-wide genotype sharing rather than known family structure.
F(x)=P(X≤x) determining interval probabilities—used in rank-based p-values and QQ overlays.
Fusion of cytoplasm in fertilization (partner to karyogamy).
Study of chromosome number, structure, and segregation—classically via karyotyping and microscopy, now complemented by sequencing.
Pyrimidine base pairing with guanine (DNA methylation commonly occurs on C in CpG).
Tai-speaking group in southwestern China referenced as example population label in ethnic categorization discussions.
dbSNP is an NCBI-hosted database of small genetic variants, including SNPs and short indels, with stable identifiers (rsIDs) used for variant naming and cross-study harmonization.

Decision curve analysis evaluates a prediction model (e.g. one including a polygenic risk score) by plotting the net benefit of using the model to treat or screen individuals across a range of risk thresholds, compared with treating all or none.

A deep generative model is a neural network that defines or approximates a distribution over high-dimensional data—images, sequences, tabular features, or count matrices—using architectures such as variational autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, normalizing flows, a...

Deep learning refers to machine learning with neural networks that contain many layers (deep architectures), trained end-to-end on large datasets; common building blocks include convolutional, recurrent, graph, and transformer layers, often pretrained with self-supervised obje...
Effective number of independent pieces of information in a statistic; inflates or deflates critical values in t, chi-square, and F reference distributions.
Conversion of arginine to citrulline on proteins (PAD-mediated); regulatory modification context.
A deletion is a variant in which one or more bases present in the reference genome are absent in the sample sequence at a locus.

Scaled parameter summarizing genetic drift strength; may differ greatly from census size.

Subdivision of a period; e.g. Holocene within Quaternary.

Deviation of estimate from target parameter—not “coding error.” Contextualizes sample-driven MSE and SE reporting.

The degree to which a genotype produces a phenotype (severity or spectrum), distinct from penetrance which is probability of any phenotype.
Ratio of scaled chi-squares—null reference for ANOVA F tests and variance ratios.

Formal claim tested with data—the causal SNP being association-null is a hypothesis in fine-mapping.
Rule deciding reject/retain null using a statistic and reference distribution—GWAS scans millions of correlated tests.

IBS0 is the proportion of markers at which two individuals share zero alleles identical by state. In relationship inference, it is especially useful for distinguishing parent-offspring pairs from full siblings.

Two alleles are identical by state (IBS) if they have the same nucleotide (or same coded genotype) at a marker, regardless of whether they were inherited from a common ancestor. IBS is observed directly from genotypes; IBD is inferred from IBS patterns across many markers.

Imputation quality metrics summarize how confidently genotypes were inferred at each variant (e.g. MaCH/Minimac Rsq, IMPUTE-style INFO). They guide filtering before association testing; at low frequency, standard metrics can be miscalibrated, motivating recalibration methods.

In-context learning is the ability of a large language model to adapt its behavior from examples or instructions placed in the prompt (the “context”) without gradient updates—sometimes called few-shot or many-shot prompting when several labeled examples are provided.
Paralogs arising by duplication after a speciation node on the subtree—tree reconciliation jargon.
Strain produced by repeated consanguineous mating homogenizing backgrounds (model organisms / plant genetics).
Mating pattern increasing IBD probability within individuals beyond random pair expectations.

The inbreeding coefficient F measures whether an individual carries two alleles identical by descent (IBD) more often than expected under random mating; for a locus or averaged across markers it quantifies departure from Hardy-Weinberg heterozygosity. In sample QC, estimated F...
Fitness decline under increased homozygosity exposing recessive load.
Number of new disease events in a population over person-time (rate) or a defined period; contrasts with prevalence for chronic traits.
An indel is a small insertion or deletion of bases relative to a reference genome. The term usually refers to short events rather than large structural rearrangements.
Factorization p(A,B)=p(A)p(B) or orthogonality of information—underlies naive permutation assumptions if unmet.
Repeated draws sharing law without coupling—idealized for bootstrap theory though genotypes are correlated.
Predictor or covariate term on RHS—genotype dosage, sex, age, and PCs in GWAS formulas.
Drawing population conclusions from samples using models, tests, and intervals—extends descriptive summaries central to GWAS reporting.

An insertion is a variant in which one or more bases are present in the sample sequence relative to the reference genome at a given locus.

Philosophical stance treating models as instruments rather than literal truth—meta-point in interpreting polygenic scores.
Boundary element blocking enhancer–promoter communication or heterochromatin spread.
Cross between heterozygous F1 individuals producing recombinant F2 segregation.
Between annotated genes—can still harbor regulatory sequence and structural variants affecting GWAS interpretation.

ICD codes are standardized diagnosis and health-state labels published by the World Health Organization—commonly ICD-9-CM, ICD-10, or ICD-11 in clinical and claims data. They underpin case definitions in biobanks, registries, and PheWAS pipelines, often mapped to aggregates su...

Introgression is the movement of alleles from one diverged lineage or species into another’s gene pool through hybridization and backcrossing, producing mosaic genomes with tracts of foreign ancestry embedded in a predominantly native background—distinct from long-standing adm...
Admixture transferring alleles across species boundaries via backcrossing—stronger emphasis than generic introgression.
Intervening sequence removed from pre-mRNA by splicing.
Within intronic sequence—many splicing and regulatory variants map intronically.
An inversion is a structural variant in which a genomic segment is reversed in orientation relative to the reference genome.
Period after Bronze Age with iron metallurgy impacting settlement and trade routes.
Chromosome composed of two genetically identical arms via misdivision around the centromere.
Intersection-over-union overlap for sets—used for pathway, gene-set, and peak overlap summaries.
Leave-one-out resampling bias/variance approximation for estimators—historical alternative to bootstrap in some variance estimates.

Joint fine-mapping analyzes association signals for two or more traits in the same locus simultaneously—using shared summary statistics, correlated priors, or multi-trait Bayes factors—to narrow credible sets and assess whether traits share causal variants.
Japanese hunter-gatherer/fisher archaeological complex preceding Yayoi farming influx.

A Jupyter Notebook is an interactive document mixing code, text, and outputs in cells, executed by a selected kernel (e.g. Python or R); notebooks document exploratory GWAS plots, QC steps, and tutorial-style reanalyses in a linear, shareable format.

JupyterLab is the next-generation web interface for the Jupyter ecosystem—multi-document workspaces, terminals, text editors, and notebook views—serving as an IDE-style front end for the same notebook and kernel model as classic Jupyter Notebook.
Mesozoic period often cited in public evolution narratives.

A nonparametric estimator of the survival function—the probability of remaining event-free up to time t—from censored time-to-event data, usually displayed as a step function with confidence intervals. It describes marginal survival in patient or cohort subgroups without assig...
Fusion of nuclei following plasmogamy/cytogamy to form a diploid nucleus.

A karyotype is the visual or systematic description of an individual’s chromosomes—number, size, banding pattern, and large structural rearrangements—usually from metaphase spreads or genome-wide copy-number inference.
Concordance-based rank correlation robust to outliers; alternative to Pearson/Spearman in small samples.
Thousand-year unit common in late Pleistocene chronology.
One thousand base pairs (or bases) along a single strand in common genomics usage.

Major rank below domain historically grouping plants, animals, fungi, etc.
Majority ethnolinguistic group of Vietnam; example regional ethnicity term in terminology lists.

Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student network to match the outputs (soft probability targets or intermediate representations) of a larger teacher model, transferring behavior with fewer parameters or faster inference—often summarized as “distillation.”
Preferred context around the start codon influencing translation initiation efficiency.
Tail heaviness of a distribution relative to Gaussian—diagnostic for QQ-plot fat tails after population stratification.

A large language model is a neural network trained on vast text to predict the next token (or span), typically using a transformer architecture; at scale it can generate fluent prose, summarize documents, translate, and follow instructions, with capabilities that depend on arc...

Lassosum fits polygenic scores by applying penalized regression (lasso-style shrinkage) to GWAS summary statistics while accounting for linkage disequilibrium via a reference panel, producing sparse or dense weight sets depending on the penalty.
Cold stadial reshaping human refugia and migration corridors; frequent ancient DNA time slice.
Model averaging K subpopulations with latent assignment—sensitive analysis for population stratification and QTL heterogeneity.

In pleiotropy research, a latent genetic variable is an unobserved factor that captures shared genetic influence across multiple measured traits—estimated, for example, via factor analysis, Genomic SEM, or related multivariate models on GWAS summary data.
Pan-regional identity label in the Americas overlapping with Hispanic categories in metadata.
Mendelian principle that one allele’s phenotype can mask the other in a heterozygote at a diallelic locus (dominant vs recessive relationship).
Alleles of different genes assort independently in gametes when loci are unlinked (Mendel’s second law; assumes no LD).
Allele pairs separate into gametes so each gamete carries one allele per locus (Mendel’s first law).

The LD score of a variant is the sum of LD r² between that SNP and all other variants in a reference panel (optionally restricted by distance). Variants in regions of high LD have large LD scores because they tag many neighbors.

LD score regression (LDSC) regresses GWAS χ² statistics on LD scores; its intercept quantifies inflation deviating from polygenic signal, and its slope relates to SNP heritability. Bivariate LDSC estimates genetic correlation between traits from summary statistics.

The learning rate sets the step size (or schedules its scale) for parameter updates during optimization; too large a rate can diverge, too small can stall or overfit slowly. Modern pipelines often use warmup, decay, or per-parameter schemes in adaptive optimizers such as Adam.
Extreme k-fold where each observation serves once as its own validation fold—expensive but nearly unbiased in small n.
A latent continuous risk scale postulated for threshold traits; only individuals above a threshold show the binary phenotype.

A model where discrete disease status arises when unobserved liability crosses a threshold; motivates liability-scale inference in genetics.
Proportion ever experiencing a condition up to a given age or survey; differs from point or period prevalence.

LiftOff is a tool that projects gene annotation from one genome assembly to another by aligning gene sequences and introns to the target assembly, preserving splice structure where possible. It is used when a reference is updated (e.g. GRCh37 to GRCh38) or when comparing close...

LiftOn is a method that combines DNA and protein alignments to transfer or refine gene annotation between assemblies, aiming to correct errors that arise when annotation is lifted by nucleotide alignment alone. It extends the LiftOff family of approaches for more accurate CDS...
LiftOver converts genomic coordinates between reference assemblies (for example GRCh37/hg19 to GRCh38/hg38) using alignment chain files, via UCSC's liftOver tool or equivalent APIs.
Function of parameters given observed data proportional to data probability—maximized in MLE and used in Bayes numerators.
Formal expression ℓ(θ|data) optimized in inference—forms core of mixed-model REML in GWAS.
Compares maximized likelihoods of nested models via approximate χ² reference—tests variance components and nested SNP sets.

In GWAS, a linear mixed model regresses the phenotype on each variant while including random effects with covariance proportional to a genetic relationship matrix (kinship), jointly modeling population structure and cryptic relatedness.
Linkage disequilibrium (LD) is the non-random correlation of alleles at different loci.

An LD proxy is a genetic variant that stands in for another variant because the two are correlated through linkage disequilibrium—often summarized by r² or D′—so association or instrument signal at one SNP partly reflects the other.

A lipid quantitative trait locus (lipid QTL) is a genetic variant associated with a specific lipid species or lipidomic feature—often from mass spectrometry lipidomics—rather than only clinical total cholesterol or LDL-C.

The lipidome is the complete set of lipid species in a biosample (e.g. plasma, tissue), profiled by mass spectrometry–based lipidomics platforms that resolve molecular lipid classes and chain compositions.
Lipidomics is the systematic measurement and analysis of lipid molecules and their distributions across pathways, often integrated with genetics as lipidome-wide association studies.

In large language models, hallucination refers to fluent outputs that are false, unsupported, or fabricated relative to the user’s sources—such as invented citations, wrong equations, or allele directions that do not appear in the data.

Local ancestry assigns each chromosomal segment of an admixed individual to one of several source ancestral populations (e.g. African vs. European along the genome), typically inferred with haplotype reference panels and models such as RFMix, LAMP, or FLARE.

A locus (plural loci) is a specific position or region in the genome, often identified by a chromosomal coordinate or a named gene interval. In association studies, a “locus” usually refers to the genomic neighborhood around a lead variant.
Different genes can cause the same phenotype; variants at distinct loci yield similar clinical presentations.
Binary (or ordinal) GLM with logit link—dominant GWAS disease association framework produces log OR estimates.
Autonomous retrotransposon class abundant in mammalian genomes; mobilizes via reverse transcription.
RNA longer than ~200 nt without a strong protein-coding reading frame; many regulate chromatin and splicing.

Long short-term memory (LSTM) is a gated recurrent neural network cell that maintains a separate cell state and uses input, forget, and output gates to propagate information across many time steps, reducing vanishing-gradient problems in long sequences.

Long-read RNA-seq uses sequencing reads that often span full-length or near-full-length cDNA molecules (e.g. from PacBio Iso-Seq or Oxford Nanopore), improving resolution of isoforms, complex splice patterns, and fusion transcripts compared with short-read RNA-seq alone.

Long-read sequencing produces reads that are much longer than standard short-read platforms, often spanning kilobases or more. These reads can better resolve structural variation, repetitive regions, and haplotypes.

Somatic or germline reduction to homozygosity at a locus—often via deletion or mitotic recombination—revealed in tumor or pedigree contexts.

A loss-of-function variant is a variant predicted to severely reduce or abolish the function of a gene product. This category often includes nonsense, frameshift, and essential splice-site variants, though definitions vary by annotation pipeline.
Sequences with biased composition or repetitiveness; can complicate alignment and variant calling.

Low-pass sequencing is whole-genome sequencing performed at low average coverage, often below standard deep WGS, with genotypes later refined by imputation. It trades per-sample certainty for lower cost and larger sample size.

Machine learning is a set of methods that fit predictive or generative models from data by optimizing an objective (loss or likelihood), rather than encoding all rules by hand; it spans supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised, and reinforcement learning, implemented with alg...

MAGMA is a software package for gene-level and gene-set analysis using GWAS summary statistics together with an LD reference panel. It maps variant-level associations to genes, aggregates signal while accounting for LD, and tests whether predefined gene sets or tissue-expressi...
Frequency of the more common allele; complement of MAF at bi-allelic sites.

A Manhattan plot displays −log10(p-value) for each tested variant along chromosomal position, with chromosome segments often colored alternately. It visualizes genome-wide association strength and highlights distinct loci as vertical stacks of correlated SNPs.
Integrated likelihood over nuisance parameters—Bayes factors and REML target related quantities.
Memory-one stochastic process transitioning among states—background for MCMC samplers and coalescent limits.
Sampling scheme drawing dependent posterior samples—used in Bayesian fine-mapping and some HMM posteriors.

Gene expressed primarily from the maternal allele under imprinting control.

Matplotlib is a foundational Python plotting library for static, publication-quality figures. It provides a MATLAB-style state interface and an object-oriented API; many genetics workflows build Manhattan-style and diagnostic plots on Matplotlib or use higher-level wrappers.

Matrix factorization approaches in pleiotropy analysis decompose GWAS effect matrices (variants × traits) or related structures into lower-rank components—latent factors or sparse patterns—that summarize shared cross-trait genetic effects.
Point estimate maximizing posterior density—bridges Bayesian posteriors with point-estimate pipelines.
Principle choosing parameter values maximizing likelihood—allele effect point estimates often ML or REML.
Procedure producing ML estimators with asymptotic normal approximations—basis for score and Wald tests.

The mean absolute error (MAE) averages absolute differences between predicted and observed values: (1/n) Σ |yᵢ − ŷᵢ|. It shares units with the outcome, downweights extreme residuals less than MSE, and is easy to interpret for continuous phenotypes or dosage predictions.

The mean squared error (MSE) averages squared residuals: (1/n) Σ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)². Squaring emphasizes large errors and yields a loss aligned with Gaussian likelihood under standard assumptions; RMSE is the square root of MSE, restoring units of the outcome.

In genetic association, effect measures link genotype to phenotype: regression coefficients for quantitative traits; odds ratios in logistic case-control models; relative risk in cohort designs; hazard ratios in time-to-event analyses.
Middle order statistic robust to extreme phenotypes—sometimes preferred for skewed lab traits.
Million-year unit for macroevolutionary depths in comparative genomics.
One million base pairs; convenient scale for chromosome-band-scale features and LD blocks.
Two division cycles that halve ploidy and shuffle haplotypes for sexual reproduction.

A Mendelian disease is caused by high-penetrance variants in one or a few genes and typically follows predictable inheritance patterns (autosomal dominant/recessive, X-linked) in families.

Core Mendelian rules—segregation, dominance, and independent assortment—that describe transmission at single-gene resolution under idealized assumptions.

European Mesolithic hunter-fisher-gatherer interval between Paleolithic and Neolithic.
Dinosaur-dominated era between Paleozoic and Cenozoic; distant mammalian genome context.

A metabolite quantitative trait locus (metaboQTL) is a genetic variant associated with the level of one or more small-molecule metabolites, usually from NMR or mass spectrometry profiling of plasma or urine. Genome-wide surveys are often called metabolome-wide association stud...

The metabolome is the complete set of small-molecule metabolites present in a biosample (e.g. plasma, urine), as profiled by mass spectrometry or NMR. It reflects downstream biochemistry of genotype, diet, microbiome, and environment.
Collective genomic content of a mixed microbial community sampled from an environment or body site without culturing individual strains.

Metagenomics is the sequencing and analysis of DNA from mixed microbial communities without culturing individual species, yielding taxonomic profiles, gene content, and strain-level variation from samples such as stool or oral swabs.
Stage where chromosomes align on the metaphase plate before segregation.
Covalent addition of methyl groups—on DNA (5mC) or proteins (e.g. arginine/lysine)—with regulatory consequences.

A methylation quantitative trait locus (mQTL; often written meQTL) is a genetic variant associated with DNA methylation level at one or more CpG sites or regions, typically measured by array or bisulfite sequencing in a relevant tissue or cell type.

The microbiome is the community of microorganisms (bacteria, archaea, viruses, fungi) and their collective genomes in a habitat such as the gut, oral cavity, or skin, often profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing or shotgun metagenomics.
Small post-transcriptional regulators binding target mRNAs to repress translation or destabilize transcripts.
A microsatellite is a short tandem repeat, typically with repeat units of 1 to 6 base pairs. In modern genomics, microsatellite and STR are often used interchangeably.
Regional identity label appearing in surveys; overlaps genetically with West Asian and North African structure.
Duration unit in paleontology and divergence time figures.

Miniprot is a fast aligner that maps protein sequences to a genome while allowing splice boundaries, analogous to spliced aligners for transcripts. It is used in annotation pipelines to project protein evidence onto DNA and to support gene prediction and comparative annotation.

A minisatellite is a tandem repeat with a longer repeat unit than a microsatellite, historically often on the order of roughly 10 to 100 base pairs. Copy number can vary substantially across individuals.

The minor allele count is the total number of copies of the minor allele observed for a variant across genotyped individuals (twice the number of homozygotes plus heterozygotes carrying that allele). Tools such as PLINK offer --mac / --max-mac filters alongside MAF.

The minor allele frequency is the frequency of the less common allele at a variant in a defined sample or population; for standard bi-allelic SNPs it lies in (0, 0.5]. (Some software reports alternate-allele frequency on [0, 1] relative to a reference base instead of MAF.)
Epoch of diversification of Old World apes affecting hominoid calibration debates.
A missense variant is a coding variant that changes the amino acid specified by a codon. Its functional impact can range from benign to strongly damaging.

Maternally inherited circular genome encoding key oxidative phosphorylation components; separate analysis from autosomal GWAS.
Somatic cell division maintaining diploidy (absent recombination between homologs as in meiosis I).
Micrococcal nuclease digestion with sequencing maps nucleosome positions and phased arrays—higher resolution than bulk accessibility alone.

Most frequent or density peak value—describes categorical phenotype baselines.

Variant altering penetrance or severity of another locus’s phenotype.

Controlled primarily by variation at a single gene (Mendelian architecture).
A locus with effectively no common variation in the surveyed population (or a single prevalent allele).
Loss of one chromosome from the diploid pair (2n−1 for that chromosome).
Identical twins from one zygote sharing nuclear genome absent somatic mosaicism.
Two or more genetically distinct cell lineages in one individual after development begins.
Designs or samples including several ancestries with explicit proportional or structured representation.

Multi-omics jointly measures and integrates two or more molecular layers—commonly genome, transcriptome, proteome, metabolome, epigenome, and microbiome—within the same individuals or matched cohorts.

Multi-trait GWAS jointly models association with two or more traits—using summary-statistic correlation structure, multivariate mixed models, or related frameworks—to boost power, estimate shared genetic architecture, and characterize cross-trait effects at loci.

A multiallelic variant is a site with more than one alternative allele relative to the reference at the same genomic position. This contrasts with the simpler biallelic representation used in many GWAS pipelines.

Influenced by multiple genetic and environmental factors; overlaps with complex trait language in clinical genetics.

A multilayer perceptron (MLP) is a feedforward neural network of fully connected layers with nonlinear activations; it maps a fixed-size input vector to outputs and is often used as a head on top of embeddings from CNNs, RNNs, or transformers.

A multimodal model consumes or generates more than one modality—e.g. text, images, audio, tabular clinical fields, or omics-derived tensors—often with shared embedding spaces and cross-attention or fusion layers rather than isolated encoders per channel.
Extension of binomial to K outcome counts—models allelic or karyotype category tallies.

Allele or strain carrying a defined mutation relative to a reference.
Heritable DNA sequence alteration; in GWAS often contrasted with polymorphism by frequency or functional classification.
Expected de novo mutation probability per generation per site or genome-wide.
Events that cannot jointly occur—allelic coding enforces mutually exclusive genotype classes at a site.

Nanopore sequencing passes single DNA strands through a protein pore and infers bases from electrical signals, producing long reads (often tens of kilobases) with portable instruments and real-time output.

Narrow-sense heritability is the proportion of phenotypic variance attributable to additive genetic effects alone. It is commonly denoted h^2 and is the heritability quantity most directly connected to standard GWAS and prediction models.
US OMB ethnicity grouping for Pacific peoples; high linguistic and genetic diversity within.
Log base e transforming likelihoods, odds ratios, and some variance-stabilizing transforms; appears in logistic and Cox GWAS output layers.

Western Eurasian archaic humans; a major archaic admixture source in non-African modern genomes.
Overdispersed count model with extra variance parameter—RNA-seq read-count GLMs before pseudobulk simplifications.

Farming and sedentism transition sampled densely in ancient genomics.

Net reclassification improvement summarizes how much a prediction model with an added predictor (e.g. a polygenic risk score) changes risk categories relative to a baseline model, net of incorrect moves across categories; it complements discrimination metrics such as AUC.

A neural network is a parametric function built from layers of connected units (nodes) with adjustable weights; training uses labeled or unlabeled data and a loss function, typically optimized by gradient-based methods so the network approximates a mapping from inputs to outputs.
Framework emphasizing drift and mutation on most molecular differences; selection on fewer sites.
Short-read massively parallel sequencing generation dominating GWAS companion RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, and WGS since ~2005.
Aromatic base moiety in nucleotides classified as purines (A, G) or pyrimidines (C, T/U).
Gene producing functional RNA without a protein product (e.g. many lncRNAs).
RNA functional product not serving as mRNA template—includes rRNA, tRNA, miRNA, lncRNA, etc.
Dominant DSB repair pathway ligating ends without a long homology template; can create indels at breakpoints.
A noncoding variant is a variant outside protein-coding sequence, such as in intronic, intergenic, untranslated, promoter, or enhancer regions. Many GWAS signals map to noncoding sequence.
A nonsense variant is a coding variant that introduces a premature stop codon, potentially truncating the encoded protein.
Surveillance eliminating mRNAs with premature stop codons; modulates severity of nonsense variants.
Gaussian bell curve underpinning linear models, many CLT approximations, and GRAM linear mixed theory at scale.
Regional label across Maghreb and adjacent areas with distinct North African genetic structure.
Polymer of nucleotides—DNA or RNA—carrying genetic or regulatory information.
Base linked to sugar (ribose or deoxyribose) lacking phosphate attachments.
Activated nucleotide substrates for polymerases; includes ATP, GTP, CTP, UTP for RNA and dNTPs for DNA.
Basic chromatin unit: DNA wrapped around a histone octamer.
Monomer of nucleic acids: nitrogenous base, sugar, and phosphate; sequences define genetic variation.
Ordered string of nucleotide symbols representing DNA or RNA including ambiguity codes; basic data type for alignment and variant representation.
Default maintained model—typically no genetic effect at a tested SNP under a frequentist association test.

The observed scale is the scale on which a trait is directly analyzed in the sample, such as a measured quantitative phenotype or the sampled 0/1 case-control outcome. For binary traits, heritability on the observed scale depends on ascertainment and case fraction.
Ratio of event probability to non-event probability for a binary outcome; GWAS logistic models estimate allelic effects on the log odds scale.

The odds ratio compares the odds of disease between genotype groups; in GWAS it is typically the per-allele OR from logistic regression in unrelated case-control data (coding one allele as the effect).
Short lagging-strand DNA pieces later ligated during replication.
Transition from Eocene hothouse toward cooler Miocene climates.
Short synthetic single-stranded DNA or RNA molecule (primers, probes, oligo therapies).

The omnigenic model proposes that for many complex traits, essentially all genes expressed in disease-relevant cells can influence the trait through highly interconnected regulatory networks, so that most genetic heritability is spread across subtle effects genome-wide rather...

An open reading frame is a contiguous span of codons from a start to a stop signal that could be translated into a protein if ribosomes initiate there. Annotation distinguishes primary CDS ORFs from overlapping or alternative ORFs; not every ORF is biologically translated.
An operating-system process is an executing program instance with its own virtual address space, resources, and one or more threads managed by the operating system.

Optimal transport in single-cell analysis treats two populations of cells (e.g. control vs perturbed, or two time points) as distributions and finds a minimum-cost coupling that maps cells or mass between them. It underlies trajectory alignment, perturbation effect estimation,...

An optimizer is an algorithm that applies gradients from backpropagation to update parameters—classic SGD, momentum, Adam, AdamW, or second-order approximations—often controlling step size via a learning rate schedule and sometimes decoupled weight decay.
Rank between class and family organizing related families.
Site licensed for replisome assembly initiating bidirectional DNA synthesis.

Orthologs are homologous genes (or sequences) in different species that arose by speciation from a single ancestral gene and typically retain related function. They contrast with paralogs, which arise by duplication within a lineage.
Orthologous genes or sequences are homologs that diverged because of a speciation event; see Ortholog.
Model where anatomically modern humans expanded from Africa in the Late Pleistocene carrying and encountering archaic admixture.
Paralogs duplicated before the speciation separating compared taxa in a gene tree–species tree reconciliation.
Heterozygote phenotype exceeds both homozygote phenotypes for a trait.
Model fitting noise leading to poor generalization—risk when over-parameterizing polygenic predictors without proper CV.
Female gamete (egg cell) contributing cytoplasm and maternal organelles including mitochondria.
Probability under null of observing a test statistic at least as extreme—misinterpreted often; needs multiple-testing context.
Label for Oceanian populations excluding Native Hawaiian in some schemas; heterogeneous.

Paired-end sequencing reads both ends of the same DNA fragment, producing two reads with known orientation and approximate insert size. This provides more positional information than single-end sequencing.
Earliest Cenozoic epoch immediately following the K-Pg boundary.
Upper and earlier Paleolithic hunter-gatherer contexts predating farming expansions.
Early animal and plant diversification; far predates human evolution but appears in textbook trees.
Variant whose flanking or inserted sequence shows near-palindrome structure relevant to some mutational mechanisms.

Pan-UK Biobank denotes large-scale genome-wide association analyses in UK Biobank that stratify or jointly model multiple ancestry groups within the resource, aiming to reduce European-centric bias in discovery and to characterize ancestry-enriched or ancestry-specific effects...

pandas is a Python library for tabular data—DataFrames and Series—with indexing, alignment, group-by aggregation, merges, and time-series utilities. In genomics it is a common way to manipulate variant lists, sample metadata, summary statistics, and annotation tables before or...
Graph or multi-reference representation of a species capturing structural and sequence variation beyond one linear reference—relevant as T2T and graph references enter alignment.
Study of pangenome variation across isolates or haplotypes including accessory sequences absent from a single reference.

Paralogs are homologous genes related by duplication within a genome or lineage—segmental or whole-genome duplication, tandem arrays, or retrocopy—after which copies can diverge in sequence, regulation, or function. They differ from orthologs, which track speciation events bet...
Paralogous genes arise by duplication within a lineage and are homologous, but are not orthologs across species; see Paralog.
Fixed but unknown quantity indexing a family of distributions—the causal allele effect size is modeled as a parameter in association regression.
Derivative of a multivariate function holding other inputs constant—used in optimization and Fisher-scoring for GLMMs.
Molar pregnancy with maternal and extra paternal contributions—distinct genetic etiology from complete mole.

Participation bias arises when individuals who enroll in a study (e.g. a biobank) differ systematically from the source population in genetics, health, or socioeconomic factors, so association and prediction estimates may not generalize and can interact with collider structures.
Gene expressed primarily from the paternal allele under imprinting control.
The potential of a variant or allele to contribute to disease in appropriate contexts (distinct from pathogenic classification in clinical databases).

Pathway (or gene-set) analysis aggregates association evidence across variants mapped to genes and then to predefined sets (pathways, GO terms, curated disease sets), testing whether a set is enriched for association signal.
Computational step defining enriched intervals from read pileups—used for ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, DNase-seq, and similar tracks feeding eQTL colocalization priors.
Linear correlation on raw or transformed scales; appears in genetic correlation and trait correlation analyses.

A pedigree is a recorded family relationship structure showing how individuals are biologically related across generations. In genetics, pedigrees provide expected relatedness patterns such as parent-offspring, siblings, and more distant relatives.
The probability that a given genotype manifests a phenotype (or trait definition) by a given age or in a given population context.
Processes colonizing or spreading into a region—timing inferred via aDNA and demography.
Covalent amide linkage joining amino acids during translation.
Cutpoint leaving a stated fraction of the reference distribution below—used for PRS thresholds and normalization.
Genomic neighborhood around the centromere often enriched for repeats and altered recombination.
Named interval within an era; e.g. Quaternary in Cenozoic.
