PGEN is the primary binary genotype format used by PLINK 2, accompanied by .pvar for variant metadata and .psam for sample metadata. It is designed for large modern cohorts and can store hard calls, dosages, missingness, and some phased information more flexibly than the older...
Eon from Cambrian explosion onward with abundant macrofossils.

PheCode is a hierarchical grouping of ICD diagnosis codes into clinically meaningful phenotypes for electronic health record and biobank research. It collapses many ICD variants into broader disease groups (and can split combined codes), easing PheWAS and multi-phenotype analy...

The phenome is the complete set of observable traits, disease diagnoses, laboratory values, and other phenotypic measurements that can be ascribed to an individual or cohort—often spanning electronic health records, biobank fields, and standardized ontologies.
PheWAS systematically tests a set of genetic variants (often trait-associated SNPs) against many phenotypes in a biobank or EHR-linked cohort, revealing pleiotropy and phenotypic profiles of alleles.

Phenomics is the large-scale, often automated acquisition and analysis of phenotypes—analogous to how genomics treats DNA—spanning deep clinical phenotyping, imaging, wearables, and structured EHR extraction.

A phenotype is an observable characteristic or measured outcome for an individual—continuous (e.g. height), binary (case-control), ordinal, survival, or multivariate. In GWAS it is the outcome or covariate linked to genotypes in the association model.

Phenotype normalization is preprocessing of trait values—often covariate adjustment, scaling, or rank-based inverse normal transformation—so that association tests meet modeling assumptions and are comparable across cohorts.
The same genotype can yield different clinical features or severity across individuals (opposite emphasis vs pleiotropy wording).
Kinase-driven addition of phosphate groups regulating protein activity and signaling cascades.
Inference of evolutionary trees or networks from heritable character data—often molecular sequences.

A phylogeny is an inferred evolutionary tree (or network) relating taxa or sequences, with branches representing descent from common ancestors and lengths often reflecting time or sequence divergence. Methods include distance, parsimony, likelihood, and Bayesian inference on a...
Major rank below kingdom grouping related classes (zoology) or divisions (botany legacy).
PI_HAT is a PLINK summary statistic for pairwise relatedness that approximates the proportion of the genome shared identical by descent. It is commonly estimated as P(IBD=2) + 0.5 x P(IBD=1).
Small RNAs partnering PIWI proteins silencing transposable elements especially in germline.
Fusion of cytoplasm between mating cells (fungi) analogous to early fertilization steps.

Pleiotropy is the phenomenon whereby one genetic variant, gene, or locus affects more than one trait or disease. It is central to interpreting overlapping GWAS signals, genetic correlations, and causal inference.

Pleiotropy dissection refers to analytical approaches that partition or explain how a variant or locus influences multiple traits—for example by distinguishing mediation through one trait versus independent effects, joint modeling of traits, or integrating functional and multi...

PLINK is a free, open-source command-line toolkit for large-scale genotype data: format conversion, quality control, linkage disequilibrium, principal components, relatedness, association testing, clumping, and related post-processing. PLINK 1.9 extends the original Purcell et...
Epoch preceding Pleistocene glaciations; early hominin fossil ages.
Number of complete chromosome sets per cell (n, 2n, 3n, etc.).
Count model with mean=variance for rare events—baseline for sparse variant counts in windows.

Polars is a DataFrame library (Rust core, Python and other bindings) designed for fast out-of-core and parallel query execution via lazy plans and explicit dtypes. Teams use it as an alternative to pandas for large summary-statistics scans, VCF-adjacent tables, and ETL before...
Mating system where females mate with multiple males; alters variance of male reproductive success.
General plural-marriage system umbrella including polygyny and polyandry in demographic models.
Controlled by many genetic variants of small effect across the genome.

Polygenic risk score portability describes how well a score trained in one population (base GWAS and LD reference) predicts in another ancestry or environment. Poor portability arises from allele frequency differences, LD mismatch, effect heterogeneity, and unequal representat...

The Polygenic Score (PGS) Catalog is an open database of published polygenic scores and their performance metrics, harmonized metadata, and links to associated traits and publications. It supports reproducibility and systematic comparison of PRS across diseases and populations.
Mating system where males mate with multiple females; affects Ne and linkage selection.
Enzymatic amplification of a DNA target between primers; basis of many genotyping and sequencing prep workflows.
Common variant conventionally above an arbitrary frequency threshold in a population.
Polymer chain of nucleotides—DNA or RNA backbone with bases.
Chain of amino acids; may fold to functional protein after PTMs.
More than two complete haploid sets in a cell lineage (e.g. triploid, tetraploid).
Condition of multiple whole-genome copies beyond diploidy; sometimes pathogenic in humans.
Hypothetical set of individuals or measurements a study aims to generalize to—inference targets sampling and ascertainment (see Biological Population for the interbreeding-group sense in genetics).

Population descriptors in genomics are the labels used to group participants—such as genetic ancestry, race, ethnicity, geography, or language—and the rules for how those labels are collected, harmonized, and reported. Major guidance (e.g. U.S. National Academies consensus stu...

Population expansion is sustained growth in census or effective population size, which tends to increase genetic diversity, shorten haplotypes relative to equilibrium expectations, and skew the site-frequency spectrum toward rare variants—unless offset by selection or structure.

A population isolate is a group with reduced gene flow and often a historical bottleneck, yielding distinctive allele frequencies, extended linkage disequilibrium, and sometimes enrichment of large-effect or locally common variants. Examples in human genetics include Finland a...
Population stratification is confounding caused by ancestry-related allele frequency differences that correlate with the phenotype.

Positive selection (Darwinian selection favoring new or standing beneficial variants) increases the frequency of alleles that raise fitness. Genomic signatures can include unusually high derived allele frequency, extended haplotype homozygosity, or excess nonsynonymous relativ...
Analyses devised after seeing data—multiple comparison adjustments tighten familywise error.
Pairwise or subset comparisons after omnibus rejection—applies in ANOVA-style pathway decompositions.
Chemical change after translation—glycosylation, ubiquitination, cleavage—expanding proteome complexity.
Distribution of parameters after conditioning on observed data; underlies credible intervals in Bayesian fine-mapping.

The posterior inclusion probability (PIP) is the posterior probability that a given variant is one of the causal (or driving) variants at a locus under a Bayesian fine-mapping model. PIPs are used to rank SNPs, form credible sets, and compare methods; they are not the same as...
Probability assignment to hypotheses or models given data and prior—e.g., causal variant posterior across SNPs.

Precision (positive predictive value in binary diagnostic language) is the fraction of positive predictions that are true positives: TP / (TP + FP). It depends strongly on prevalence and threshold choice when base rates are low.
Puberty onset markedly earlier than population norms; can have monogenic contributors studied alongside population traits.
Classifier-predicted protein-truncating or strongly disruptive consequence (often integrating canonical splice, stop, frameshift) used in rare-variant burden and constraint metrics.
Human past predating written records; dominant sampling frame for many aDNA studies.

Preregistration documents the study design, hypotheses, and analysis plan before outcomes are fully known—often via registered reports or time-stamped protocols—reducing selective reporting and post hoc analytic flexibility.

Pretraining is the first, large-scale training phase where a model learns general representations from broad data—next-token prediction for text, masked modeling, contrastive image objectives, or denoising autoencoding—before fine-tuning or prompting on a downstream task.
Proportion of a population with disease or trait at a time or period; affects case–control sampling and liability-scale correction.
Cells isolated directly from tissue with limited division capacity; contrast with immortalized cell lines.
Short oligonucleotide providing a 3′ OH for polymerase extension in PCR or sequencing library prep.

Principal component analysis finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance; in GWAS, PCA of genotypes (often after LD pruning and relatedness filtering) yields ancestry axes used as covariates or for visualizing population structure.
Placed on parameters before data; regularizes effect estimates and enters colocalization frameworks.
Baseline credence on models or paths before evidence—controls stringency of Bayesian fine-mapping.
Measure of uncertainty obeying axioms—GWAS p-values and posteriors report calibrated or heuristic probabilities.
Derivative of CDF for continuous X; integrates to probabilities over intervals—likelihoods for continuous phenotypes.
Complete specification of probabilities over outcomes—allele count models reference binomial or product-binomial distributions.
Point masses p(x) summing to one—likelihood for discrete genotypes and counts.
Kolmogorov-compliant assignment of probabilities to measurable events underpinning asymptotic theory.
Mathematical foundations (measure theory) for inference—supports large-sample MLE and LRT results geneticists rely on.
Index individual ascertaining a pedigree—often first affected in segregation analysis.
Organism without a membrane-bound nucleus (e.g. bacteria); relevant for microbiome and some comparative genomics, less central to human GWAS.
Transition between prophase and metaphase when the nuclear envelope breaks down and spindle attaches.

A promoter is the DNA region immediately upstream (and sometimes downstream) of a gene’s transcription start site where the basal transcription machinery and regulatory factors assemble to initiate RNA polymerase transcription. Core promoter elements (e.g. TATA box, initiator)...

In large language model systems, a prompt is the input text (and sometimes structured metadata) sent to the model to elicit a response—ranging from a short instruction to long documents, few-shot examples, or tool schemas. It is distinct from prompt engineering, which is the d...

Prompt engineering is the practice of designing inputs (instructions, examples, format constraints) to steer a language model toward reliable outputs without changing its weights—often using role prompts, few-shot demonstrations, or structured templates.

Prompt learning (often overlapping with prompt tuning or prefix tuning) trains learnable prompt parameters—continuous vectors prepended or inserted into the model input—so that a frozen or lightly updated large model adapts to a task without full fine-tuning of all weights. It...
Integrated bacteriophage genome in a bacterial chromosome maintained latently.
First stage of mitosis/meiosis marked by chromosome condensation and other preparatory events.
Dimensionless fraction (0–1) of individuals with an attribute in a defined base population at risk.
Participants enrolled forward in time with outcomes ascertained after baseline—reduces recall bias for exposures.

A protein quantitative trait locus (pQTL) is a genetic variant associated with the plasma, serum, or tissue abundance of a protein (or peptide feature), typically mapped from affinity or mass-spectrometry proteomics relative to a genome-wide genotype scaffold.
Variant introducing premature stop, frameshift, or splice disruption removing core domain—overlaps PTV burden tests.
The proteome is the complete set of proteins—and their isoforms and modifications—present in a cell, biofluid, or tissue, often measured by mass spectrometry or affinity-based assays.

Proteomics is the large-scale study of protein abundance, interactions, and post-translational modification, typically using mass spectrometry or multiplexed affinity platforms on biofluids or tissues.
Societies on the edge of literacy—chronological grey zone in regional histories.
Integrated viral genome in a host cell (e.g. retroviral integration).

A proxy phenotype uses a related indicator of disease or trait status when direct phenotyping is missing or weak—classically, family history of disease as a surrogate in GWAS-by-proxy designs, or educational attainment proxies for cognitive traits—expanding effective sample si...

The base cohort in polygenic score analysis is the discovery sample (or meta-analysis) from which GWAS summary statistics—effect sizes, p-values, and aligned alleles—are taken to define SNP weights. It must not overlap the target cohort used for unbiased evaluation when possible.

Clumping and thresholding (C+T) is a polygenic score construction strategy: variants are first clumped to reduce linkage disequilibrium redundancy (one “index” SNP per LD block), then SNPs are included according to a series of P-value thresholds from the base GWAS, often selec...

The target cohort in polygenic score analysis is the sample with individual-level genotypes (and usually phenotypes and covariates) on which the PRS is computed and evaluated—e.g. association of the score with the trait, variance explained, or stratification by score deciles.

PRSice-2 is software for calculating polygenic scores from GWAS summary statistics and individual-level target genotypes, supporting large-scale workflows including clumping, multiple P-value inclusion thresholds, regression-based evaluation, and high-dimensional phenotype tar...
Deterministic generator sequence approximating randomness under a seed—permutes phenotypes in max-T style tests.

Pseudo-R² is a class of goodness-of-fit measures for models with non-Gaussian outcomes (e.g. logistic regression) that mimic the interpretability of R² by scaling log-likelihood improvement relative to a null model; common variants include McFadden’s and Nagelkerke’s definitions.

Pseudoautosomal regions are homologous intervals shared between the X and Y chromosomes that still undergo recombination in male meiosis. Variants in these intervals can behave differently from non-PAR X-linked loci because both sex chromosomes carry corresponding sequence.
Plural usage for pseudoautosomal intervals shared by the X and Y chromosomes. This dictionary treats Pseudoautosomal Region (PAR) as the preferred entry for the full definition.

Pseudobulk aggregation sums or averages single-cell RNA-seq counts (or normalized expression) per donor and cell type (or cluster), producing profiles that resemble bulk RNA-seq but preserve cell-type specificity. These profiles are often used for QTL mapping when per-cell spa...
Genomic segment homologous to a functional gene but with disabling mutations or lack of expression.

Pseudotime is a computational ordering of single cells along a latent axis intended to approximate progression through a biological process (e.g. differentiation or activation) when true time is unknown. It is derived from transcriptome similarity, not clock time.
Developmental transition with strong hormonally regulated timing; timing traits appear in some GWAS contexts.

pVCF (project VCF, often "population VCF" in practice) refers to a cohort-scale VCF representation optimized for large multi-sample callsets and downstream analysis workflows. Specific layout details can vary by toolchain, but the goal is efficient storage and access for very...

Python is a high-level, general-purpose language widely used for scripting and building bioinformatics and statistical-genetics pipelines. In GWAS-related work it appears in quality control, association wrappers, visualization, single-cell workflows, and machine-learning exten...

Quality control in GWAS encompasses prespecified filters and checks on samples and variants (missingness, allele frequency, HWE, relatedness, ancestry outliers, heterozygosity) and on phenotypes (outliers, consistency), plus post-association calibration checks (genomic inflati...
Generalization of percentiles indexing any fraction τ∈(0,1)—used in rank-based transforms and inverse-normal scoring.

In GWAS, a QQ plot compares quantiles of observed association test statistics (or −log10 p) to their null expectation. Under proper calibration, points follow the diagonal except for an upward tail where true associations depart from the null.
Special quantiles at 25, 50, 75%—common stratification bins for continuous covariates.
Five-way quantile split—used for QQ strata or socioeconomic grouping in meta-analyses.

R is a language and environment for statistical computing and graphics. Biostatistics and genetics communities rely on R for linear and mixed models, visualization, Bioconductor omics packages, and many published GWAS and fine-mapping workflows distributed as scripts or packages.

Race is a socially defined category, historically tied to racism and power structures, that groups people by perceived physical traits or lineage. In biomedical research it is often collected as self-report or observer assignment. It is not equivalent to genetic ancestry, thou...
Panel of cells used historically for long-range mapping via chromosome breakage—legacy mapping concept.
Bias when marine or freshwater carbon skews apparent C-14 ages; calibration issue for coastal samples.
Numeric summary of uncertain outcomes—GWAS treats observed phenotypes and coded genotypes as realized draws from stochastic models.
Random-Access Memory (RAM) is volatile main memory that stores data and program state while a computer is running, with direct access to addresses for fast reads and writes.
Experimental design randomizing interventions to estimate causal effects; genetic studies rarely randomize genotypes but RCTs motivate drug targets from GWAS.
Uses score and Fisher info avoiding full Hessian—fast approximations in some genome-wide scans.
A rare variant is a genetic variant with low population frequency, commonly defined using a minor allele frequency threshold such as less than 1% or 0.5%. The exact cutoff varies by study.

A rare variant aggregation test jointly analyzes many rare or low-frequency variants in a genetic region—typically a gene, exon set, or window—by collapsing or modeling them as a single multivariate signal. Review classifications include burden, adaptive burden, variance-compo...
Measure of disease frequency per unit person-time or per capita-time; central to incidence density and hazard intuition.
Quotient comparing two measures (e.g. incidence in exposed vs unexposed); relative risk and odds ratio are common comparative ratios.
A read is a nucleotide sequence produced by a sequencing instrument from a DNA fragment. Reads are later aligned or assembled to infer the underlying genomic sequence and variants.
Read depth is the number of sequencing reads covering a given genomic position. It is the locus-level version of coverage and directly affects confidence in the called genotype or allele.

Recall is the fraction of actual positives correctly identified: TP / (TP + FN). In medical testing it is sensitivity (true positive rate). Recall and precision trade off as classification thresholds change.
A recessive model tests association only for homozygotes of the alternate (or minor) allele compared with all other genotypes, requiring two copies to alter risk or trait mean.
Allele property where the heterozygote resembles the high-dose homozygote; requires two copies (autosomal) for trait expression in the classic definition.
Exchange between two chromosomes without net gain/loss; can disrupt genes at breakpoints.
Exchange of genetic material between homologous chromosomes (meiosis) or repair-associated reshuffling; sets correlation structure along chromosomes.
Genomic intervals with elevated meiotic crossover rates; influences LD footprint shapes and fine-mapping priors.
Crossovers per physical distance (often cM/Mb); affects LD decay with genetic distance.

A recurrent neural network (RNN) processes sequential inputs with hidden states updated at each time step, sharing parameters across positions; practical variants such as LSTM and GRU gates mitigate vanishing gradients for long dependencies.
Methyl-CpG profiling targeting restriction-enriched CpG-dense subsets; lower cost than WGBS for methylation QTL or pilot epigenetic layers.

The reference allele is the nucleotide at a site on a chosen reference genome assembly (e.g. GRCh38). In VCF/BCF it is often labeled REF; PLINK2 aligns alleles to reference when producing REF/ALT columns.

A regional plot is a locus-level visualization of association results around a lead variant. It typically shows genomic position on the x-axis, association strength on the y-axis, nearby genes, and point colors reflecting LD with the lead SNP.
Any explanatory column in a regression design matrix—including allele count encodings.

Regularization constrains a model to improve generalization and calibration: L1/L2 penalties shrink coefficients in classical prediction, while dropout, noise injection, weight decay, and early stopping play analogous roles in deep learning on high-dimensional omics inputs. In...

Relatedness summarizes how genetically similar two individuals are, usually via shared ancestry. It is operationalized with IBD probabilities, kinship coefficients, or IBS-based metrics and is estimated from genome-wide SNP data when pedigrees are incomplete.

Relatedness describes how closely individuals share alleles identical by descent (IBD); sample structure includes both known pedigrees and cryptic relatedness. Kinship and genetic relationship matrices summarize pairwise relatedness for use in QC and association models.
Relatedness coefficient usually means the IBD probability denoted r in pedigree genetics—the same quantity as the coefficient of relationship. Preferred entry: Coefficient of relatedness (r).

Relative risk is the ratio of event probabilities between two groups, such as carriers versus non-carriers of an allele. In cohort or prospective analyses it directly compares absolute risk over a fixed follow-up window or study period.

A repeat expansion is a variant in which the number of copies of a short tandem repeat motif increases beyond the usual range. These events are often difficult to capture with standard SNP-focused methods.
DNA element replicated as a unit from an origin to termination region.
Outcome minus fitted mean from a model—used in phenotype transformation and score statistics.

A response eQTL is a genetic association with gene expression that appears or changes strength when cells are stimulated or perturbed (e.g. cytokine treatment, pathogen exposure), reflecting context-dependent regulation not evident in resting baseline profiles.
Endonuclease cutting at or near specific recognition sites; foundational for cloning and some assays.
DNA sequence recognized and cut (or epigenetically protected) by a restriction enzyme.

Retrieval-augmented generation couples a language model with a retriever over a document corpus (papers, manuals, database snippets) so that answers are conditioned on fetched evidence, reducing reliance on parametric memory alone.
Historical cohort assembled from records and followed up to a past or present endpoint—efficient but sensitive to missing data and coding.
Transposable element amplifying through an RNA intermediate via reverse transcription.
RNA virus replicating via reverse transcription and integrating a provirus into host DNA.
Nucleoside containing ribose; RNA building blocks before phosphorylation.
Repeated arrays encoding rRNA genes; define nucleolar organizer regions on acrocentric short arms.
Structured catalytic and scaffold RNAs forming ribosomes for translation.

Probability of an outcome in a defined period among those at risk; absolute risk complements relative effect sizes from GWAS.
Attribute or exposure associated with higher disease probability; genetic and environmental factors are both invoked cautiously for causality.

Risk stratification is the process of grouping individuals into ordered risk categories (e.g. quantiles or clinical tiers) using predictors such as polygenic scores, family history, and conventional risk factors, often to guide prevention or screening.
RNA-seq measures transcript abundance and sequence by sequencing RNA (often cDNA) across the transcriptome, enabling gene expression quantification, isoform detection, and fusion discovery.
Removal of introns and joining exons to form mature transcripts.

RNA velocity estimates the direction and rate of change of gene expression for individual cells by contrasting spliced and unspliced mRNA counts (or related dynamical models), predicting short-term transcriptional trends along differentiation or activation processes.
Roadmap Epigenomics is a reference project that generated epigenomic maps across many primary tissues and cell types, including histone modifications, DNA methylation, and chromatin accessibility.

The root mean squared error (RMSE) is the square root of MSE, √( (1/n) Σ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)² ). It is in the same units as the outcome, so it is easier to interpret than MSE for continuous phenotypes while still penalizing large errors more than MAE does.

Rust is a systems programming language emphasizing memory safety and concurrency without a garbage collector. In genomics it backs high-performance tools and libraries (including components of modern dataframe and alignment stacks) and is increasingly used for new native bioin...

Observed subset drawn from a target population; GWAS effect estimates are conditional on sample ascertainment and size.
Sample missingness is the fraction of genotype calls missing for a given individual across assayed variants. It is the sample-level complement of call rate.
Distribution of a statistic under repeated random sampling—justifies standard errors, z-scores, and asymptotic GLMM theory.

Sanger sequencing uses chain-terminating dideoxynucleotides and capillary electrophoresis to read a single DNA sequence fragment at a time, historically the gold standard for accuracy and still common for validation.

Satellite DNA refers to highly repetitive DNA composed of many tandemly repeated sequences, often located in centromeric or pericentromeric regions. These repeats are usually grouped by repeat-unit size and genomic organization.

SCANPY is a Python library for analysis of large single-cell gene expression datasets, covering preprocessing, normalization, visualization (e.g. on embeddings), clustering, and marker discovery in a workflow often paired with AnnData objects.

Gradient of log-likelihood w.r.t. parameters—zero at MLE; drives score (Rao) tests.

scPerturb is a harmonized collection and metadata standard for single-cell perturbation datasets—combining processed expression matrices, perturbation annotations, and study covariates so models and benchmarks can be trained across many screens consistently.
seaborn is a Python visualization library built on Matplotlib with high-level functions for statistical graphics—distributions, heatmaps, and facet grids—using tidy tables (often pandas).
Near-identical duplicated multi-kb–Mb segments seeding CNV and complicating mapping.

Selection pressure is the environmental or biological force that makes some heritable traits or alleles more or less advantageous—pathogens, diet, climate, mate choice, competition, or cultural practice—thereby steering the strength and direction of natural selection over time.

DNA strand with the same 5′→3′ polarity as the mature RNA transcript (non-template coding orientation).

SKAT is a variance-component test for association between a trait and a set of rare variants in a region. It uses a kernel on the genotype matrix so that power is maintained when effects vary in direction and magnitude across variants, unlike a single-direction burden test.
Short recurring sequence pattern (often degenerate) representing binding or enzymatic preferences.
Determination of nucleotide order in a DNA or RNA template by enzymatic synthesis, ligation, or single-molecule detection—foundation technology for genotype and molecular QTL layers.

Illumina sequencing (sequencing by synthesis) uses reversible fluorescent terminators to build DNA reads on a flow cell, producing billions of short reads (typically tens to hundreds of bases) with high accuracy and throughput.
Association with sex chromosomes—often X-linked inheritance patterns with sex differences in prevalence or GWAS modeling.
A short tandem repeat is a tandem repeat with a short repeated motif, commonly 1 to 6 base pairs long. STR length often varies between individuals because of differences in repeat copy number.

Short-read sequencing generates relatively short DNA reads, typically tens to a few hundred bases long, at high throughput and low per-base cost. It is the dominant format for most large-scale WGS and WES studies.
Prefixed α controlling Type I error rate in hypothesis tests—GWAS often ties this to genome-wide thresholds.
One continuous predictor linearly related to outcome—pedagogic baseline extending to multiple regression in GWAS covariates.
Aggregate associations reversing when stratified—motivates ancestry adjustment and careful cohort mixing in meta-analyses.

A SNP is a DNA polymorphism where alternate alleles differ by a single nucleotide at one genomic position. SNP arrays and imputed panels overwhelmingly supply the variants tested in conventional GWAS.
An SNV is a sequence variant involving a change of one nucleotide at a single genomic position. Unlike a SNP, an SNV does not require the site to be common in the population.
ATAC-seq performed on single cells or single nuclei resolving accessibility heterogeneity and lineage-specific regulatory programs.

A single-cell eQTL (sc-eQTL) is a genetic variant associated with gene expression measured at single-cell resolution, often mapped within a defined cell type, cluster, or continuous cell state rather than in bulk tissue homogenate.

Single-cell perturbation genomics measures transcriptomic (and increasingly multi-omic) responses of individual cells to deliberate perturbations—genetic (e.g. CRISPR), chemical, or cytokine stimuli—often in pooled high-throughput designs. It complements observational atlases...
Low-input RRBS adapted to single cells for cell-type-specific methylomes in heterogeneous tissue.
Profiling transcripts in individual cells capturing heterogeneity, trajectories, and cell-type programs—often merged with GWAS loci via eQTL and single-cell eQTL frameworks.
Single-cell sequencing profiles DNA or RNA from individual cells rather than bulk tissue, revealing cell-type-specific genotypes, expression, and heterogeneity in large cell populations.
Sequencing reads from one fragment end only—cheaper but less accurate indel and insert resolution than paired-end.

PacBio single-molecule real-time (SMRT) sequencing reads DNA in long continuous fragments; HiFi reads combine long length with high accuracy and are widely used for assembly, phasing, and structural variant detection.
scRNA-seq performed on isolated nuclei—useful for frozen tissue where whole-cell capture is difficult.

Two DNA copies after replication held together until anaphase segregation.

SKAT-O is an omnibus rare-variant test that optimally combines burden-type and SKAT variance-component statistics into a single association score. It adapts when causal variants share direction (burden-like power) versus when effects are heterogeneous (SKAT-like power).
Asymmetry measure of a distribution—guides phenotype transform choice before association.

Slurm (Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) is a workload manager and job scheduler that allocates cluster resources and runs queued compute jobs on HPC systems.
~21 nt dsRNA-guided silencing in experimental and endogenous pathways.
snRNP components of the spliceosome mediating intron removal.
Guides chemical modification of rRNA and snRNA in the nucleolus.
Single-cell full-length cDNA protocol using template switching for mRNA-seq from individual cells—historically common for scRNA workflows.
Single Molecule Real-Time sequencing on zero-mode waveguides producing long reads with native molecule context (methylation on some platforms).

SNP heritability is the proportion of phenotypic variance explained by the SNPs included in, or tagged by, the data and model used in a GWAS analysis. It is usually lower than family-based heritability because it does not capture all genetic variation equally well.
A software thread is a lightweight execution path within a process. Multiple threads in one process share memory space while running concurrently on one or more CPU cores.
Mutation arising after birth in a cell lineage; contrasts with germline variants in GWAS arrays.
Coarse label for probabilistic genetic ties to a broad world region in biobanks and reference panels; distinct from social identity alone.

Monotonic rank-based correlation; robust to heavy tails in omics traits.

Speciation is the formation of reproductively isolated lineages—by geographic separation, ecological divergence, chromosomal change, or other barriers—so that gene flow between them ceases or is greatly reduced and they diverge as distinct species or incipient species over time.
Fundamental taxon for sexually reproducing organisms often defined by reproductive isolation or lineage divergence.

Specificity is the true negative rate in binary classification: TN / (TN + FP)—the fraction of negatives correctly classified as negative. Specificity and sensitivity (recall) describe operating characteristics at a fixed threshold; AUC integrates performance across thresholds.
Male gamete; typically contributes nuclear DNA and little cytoplasm.

A splice-site variant is a variant near exon-intron boundaries that may alter RNA splicing. Depending on position and context, it can disrupt normal transcript structure.
Large RNP machine catalyzing splice-site selection and intron removal.

A splicing quantitative trait locus (sQTL) is a genetic variant associated with isoform usage, exon inclusion, or junction counts—usually quantified from RNA-seq split reads or splicing arrays—rather than (or in addition to) total gene expression.
Selection against extremes maintaining intermediate trait means.
Square root of variance in same units as data—reports phenotype and effect heterogeneity.
Uncertainty scale of a statistic estimator—GWAS outputs report SE per allele effect.
σ/√n scaling for the sample mean’s sampling variability—relevant to cohort-level summaries.

Statistical genetics applies probability models and inference to related individuals and populations: heritability estimation, association mapping, polygenic prediction, and control of confounding from relatedness and population structure.

Statistical power is the probability that a test rejects the null when it is false (1 minus Type II error rate). In GWAS it depends on sample size, case-control balance, effect size, allele frequency, and the significance threshold.
Field and practice of collecting, summarizing, modeling, and inferring under uncertainty—foundation of association testing and meta-analysis.
Plains pastoral economies linked to Bronze Age migrations in ancient DNA literature.
Governed by probabilistic laws rather than fixed outputs—describes genetic drift, sequencing noise, and MCMC draws.
Collection of random variables indexed by time or space—underlies neutral models of allele frequency trajectories.
Umbrella for pre-metal lithic archaeological periods regionalized as Paleolithic/Mesolithic/Neolithic.
Variant introducing a premature termination codon (nonsense or elongation-to-stop context).
Variant removing the normal stop codon causing read-through into the 3′ UTR.

Joint system of measurement and structural equations—distinct from abbreviation clashes with “standard error mean.”

A structural variant is a large genomic alteration such as a deletion, duplication, inversion, translocation, or complex rearrangement. Structural variants often span more bases than typical SNPs or short indels.
Heavy-tailed family for small-sample test stats—reference for moderate-n linear regression CIs.
Region adjacent to telomeres; can harbor structural variation and segmental duplications.

Unexplained variation after fitting—RSS drops as predictors improve fit subject to overfitting risk.
Attachment of SUMO peptides modulating localization, stability, and interaction networks.

Invariance of a distribution about its center—assumed approximately after variance-stabilizing transforms.

A synonymous variant is a coding variant that changes the DNA sequence without changing the encoded amino acid. It is sometimes called a silent variant, although it can still affect splicing or expression.

A system prompt is a high-priority instruction block configured by the application (not the end user) that sets global behavior—role, safety rules, output format, and allowed tools—before user prompts are applied. It is one lever for policy and reproducibility across sessions.
Sequencing rearranged TCR chains to profile clonal diversity and antigen-experienced compartments—used in tumor and infection companion studies.
Studentized statistic using estimated SE—student t references moderate-sample linear models.
Nonlinear embedding visualizing high-dimensional genomics; superseded for some QC by UMAP but still cited.
Dravidian-speaking group in South Asia and diaspora; example ethnic label in surveys.
A tandem repeat is a DNA sequence motif repeated head-to-tail multiple times at the same genomic locus. The repeated unit can be short or long, and the copy number can vary between individuals.
Targeted sequencing enriches and sequences a predefined set of genomic regions, such as candidate genes, custom panels, or loci of interest, rather than the whole exome or genome.
Core promoter motif bound by TBP/TATA-binding protein in many RNA polymerase II genes.
Protective terminal repeat-rich structure of linear chromosomes; relevant to replication and stability.
Final stage of mitosis/meiosis with nuclei re-forming and chromosomes decondensing.

Temperature scales logits before a softmax when sampling from a language model: values below one sharpen the distribution (more greedy), values above one flatten it (more random). It is a decoding knob separate from training objectives or fine-tuning.
Four copies of each homologous chromosome (4n) in a conceptual full set.
Single-molecule long-read platforms (PacBio, Nanopore) enabling multi-kb reads and native modification detection complementing short-read arrays.
Millennial-scale unit in climate and archaeology timelines.
DNA pyrimidine pairing with adenine (replaced by uracil in RNA).

A token is the atomic unit an LLM’s tokenizer produces from text—often a subword piece rather than a whole word. Costs, context window limits, and rate limits are usually expressed in tokens, not characters.

Tool calling (also called function calling) is a pattern where the model emits structured requests—function name and JSON arguments—for a runtime to execute external code or APIs, then feeds results back for another model turn. It underpins many AI agents and MCP integrations.
Total squared deviations around the overall mean—numerator of baseline variance before covariates.

A training epoch is one full pass over the training dataset (or its shuffled partitions) under a given sampling protocol; practice estimates progress in epochs or steps and pairs them with validation curves, early stopping, and learning-rate schedules.

A trait is the characteristic under study (e.g. height, LDL cholesterol, disease liability). It may be measured directly as a phenotype or defined conceptually; complex traits are typically polygenic and influenced by environment.

Trajectory inference (trajectory mapping) is a class of computational methods that infer a dynamic biological process from static single-cell snapshots—ordering cells along paths or trees (e.g. differentiation, activation)—often summarized with pseudotime or branch assignments.
Factor encoded elsewhere (diffusible protein or ncRNA) acting on target loci in trans.
Across ancestries; often denotes methods or meta-analyses explicitly pan-ancestry.

Across self-identified ethnic groups; terminology in older multi-population association literature (use precise labels when possible).
TOPMed is an NHLBI-supported program that generated deep whole-genome sequencing and harmonized phenotype data across multiple cohorts to advance cardiovascular, lung, blood, and sleep research.
Factor influencing expression from another genomic location—often summarized in trans-eQTL mapping.

Synthesis of RNA from a DNA template by RNA polymerase with assorted cofactors.

The transcriptome is the complete set of RNA transcripts in a cell, tissue, or biosample at a given time, including protein-coding mRNAs and noncoding RNAs as profiled by RNA-seq, microarrays, or single-cell methods.

A TWAS tests association between a trait and genetically predicted gene expression (or other molecular traits) by combining expression prediction models from reference panels with GWAS summary statistics, aggregating signal across cis variants.

Transcriptomics is the large-scale measurement and analysis of RNA abundance, splicing, and (in single cells) cell-type-resolved expression programs, usually relative to a reference annotation or assembled transcriptome.

Transfer learning reuses representations or weights trained on a source domain or task (often large-scale pretraining) and adapts them to a target task with fine-tuning, feature extraction, or prompting, improving data efficiency when labels are scarce.
Adapter molecules delivering amino acids to ribosomes per codon anticodon pairing.

A transformer is a neural network architecture built from stacked blocks of multi-head self-attention and position-wise feedforward layers, usually with residual connections and layer normalization; positional encodings supply order information without recurrence.
Ribosome-mediated peptide synthesis decoding mRNA codons to amino acids.
A translocation is a structural rearrangement in which a genomic segment is moved to a different chromosomal location, sometimes between chromosomes.

DNA that can change genomic location or copy number via transposition mechanisms.
Mobile genetic element; DNA transposons move without RNA intermediate; retrotransposons use RNA.
Integrating multiple imperfect data sources or analytic approaches to strengthen causal claims—e.g. SNP–trait consistency across designs, populations, and omics.
Earliest Mesozoic period after end-Permian extinction recovery.
Three complete haploid sets (3n)—often lethal or severe when constitutive in humans.
Pathogenic intolerance to three functional copies of a locus or region (dosage opposite of haploinsufficiency framing).
Gain of one extra chromosome (2n+1 for that chromosome).

Attachment of ubiquitin chains targeting proteins for degradation or non-degradative signaling.
UK Biobank is a large prospective cohort and biobank with extensive genotype, health record, imaging, and lifestyle data, widely used for population-scale genetic association analyses.

UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) is a nonlinear dimension-reduction method. In genetics it is sometimes applied to PC coordinates or genotype-derived embeddings to highlight local structure in population data.
Heterozygote fitness below homozygotes—polymorphism maintenance requires spatial structure or other mechanisms.
Overly simple model missing systematic signal—raises type II error in sparse genetic architectures.
Both copies of a chromosome inherited from the same parent—reveals imprinting disorders or recessive risk.

A unique molecular identifier (UMI) is a random molecular barcode added to cDNA before PCR in many single-cell RNA-seq protocols. UMIs allow reads to be deduplicated so that quantification reflects distinct molecules rather than PCR amplification copies.

Unsupervised learning discovers structure in inputs without per-example labels—via clustering, low-dimensional embeddings, density modeling, or self-supervised pretext tasks—often as a precursor to downstream prediction or interpretation.
5′ or 3′ mRNA segments regulating stability, localization, and initiation beyond the coding ORF.

An upstream open reading frame is a short ORF in the 5′ untranslated region of a transcript, upstream of the main coding sequence. uORFs can modulate translation efficiency or mRNA stability of the primary CDS through leaky scanning, reinitiation, or regulated translation.
RNA pyrimidine replacing thymine; pairs with adenine in RNA duplexes.
U-decay chain dating used for speleothems and some fossiliferous settings.

Measurable trait or covariate column analyzed in models—phenotypes, PCs, and dosages are variables in GWAS regressions.

A variable number tandem repeat is a tandem repeat locus where individuals differ in the number of repeat units. VNTR is a broad term that has often been used especially for longer repeat units such as minisatellites.
Expected squared deviation around the mean—underpins heritability partitions and effect variance components.

A variance quantitative trait locus (varQTL or vQTL) is a genetic variant associated with variability of a molecular phenotype—such as gene expression heterogeneity across cells or individuals—rather than (or in addition to) its mean level.

Variant annotation maps genetic variants to functional and genomic context: gene symbols, consequence (missense, splice, intronic), conservation, regulatory tracks, and population frequencies. Tools include ANNOVAR, Ensembl VEP, and snpEff.

Variant calling is the process of identifying sequence differences such as SNVs and indels from aligned sequencing reads relative to a reference genome. It combines evidence from read bases, mapping, quality scores, and local haplotype context.

Variant missingness is the fraction of samples lacking a genotype call for a given SNP or variant. It is the variant-level complement of call rate.

Vertical pleiotropy describes settings where a variant affects one trait that lies on the causal path to another (e.g. a biomarker intermediate between a gene product and disease), so effects on multiple phenotypes are chained through a mediating mechanism.

The Wahlund effect is an apparent deficit of heterozygotes caused by analyzing a mixture of subpopulations with different allele frequencies as though they were a single random-mating population. It is a population-structure explanation for Hardy-Weinberg deviation.
Quadratic form using estimate and inverse Fisher information—common z-statistic for allele effects.
Coarse label for probabilistic genetic ties to a broad world region in biobanks and reference panels; distinct from social identity alone.
Whole-exome sequencing targets protein-coding exons and adjacent splice regions, enriching coding sequence for variant calling at lower cost than WGS.
Bisulfite conversion plus genome-wide sequencing for base-resolution DNA methylation at most C contexts coverage allows.

Whole-genome sequencing reads chromosomal DNA broadly (exonic, intronic, regulatory), enabling discovery of SNVs, indels, and many structural variants at base resolution depending on coverage and algorithms.

Winner's curse is the systematic over- or underestimation of genetic effect sizes for variants selected because they exceed a significance threshold, because conditioning on crossing that threshold truncates the sampling distribution of the estimate.

Wright's F_ST names Sewall Wright’s classical between-population fixation index. In this dictionary the primary discussion lives under Fixation index (FST).
Silencing one X in cis in female mammals to balance X-linked dosage with XY males.
X-linked locus including XIST that nucleates silencing on the inactive X.

XMAP is a cross-population fine-mapping method that uses genetic diversity across ancestries and explicit modeling of confounding to refine causal variant evidence within a locus, complementing single-ancestry fine-mapping and multi-ancestry SuSiE-type approaches.
Synonymous reporting with BP for sediment or bone chronologies.
Yeast vector carrying large inserts—historic clone system for long genomic fragments.
Standardized deviation using population or estimated SD—used for phenotype normalization and outlier QC.
Large-sample normal-reference test for means or proportions—approximation behind some score tests at huge n.

Diploid cell formed by gamete fusion; starting point of a new diploid organism.
